worksheet.title: When the Flag Is Clicked
worksheet.subtitle: An event is what starts a script
worksheet.learning_goal: I can read the event block that tells a script when to start.

parts.title: A script waits for its event
parts.text: A script does not run on its own — it waits for an EVENT. Clicking the green flag is an event. The orange hat block 'when green flag clicked' sits on top of a script and starts it when the flag is clicked. Bit's home is 0. Watch what the event makes Bit do.

parts.title: Click the flag
parts.prompt: The green flag is clicked, so the event happens and Bit's script runs. From home 0, forward 3. What number does Bit land on?

parts.title: No event yet
parts.prompt: Before anyone clicks the flag, the event has NOT happened. Does Bit's script run yet? Circle YES or NO. What number is Bit on?

parts.title: What is the event?
parts.prompt: Look at the orange hat block. What EVENT starts Bit's script? Write it.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: The orange hat block names the EVENT that starts a script. 'When green flag clicked' means: wait until the flag is clicked, then run. No event yet means the script has not run — Bit stays at home.

teacher_guide.title: When the Flag Is Clicked
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key
teacher_guide.footer_topic: 1. When the Flag Is Clicked — Teacher Guide

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students meet events: a set of moves is started by an event. The block on top (an orange "hat") names the event — here, "when green flag clicked". The key idea: the moves wait for their event — until the flag is clicked, nothing runs. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer needed — paper and a pencil. You read the prompts aloud. Optional: two counters on a number line 0 to 5 (green Bit, purple Pixel), and a card that says "go" you can hand over to act out sending a message.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 20 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). Point to the orange hat: "this set of moves waits until the green flag is clicked." Click it, then run the moves.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — the flag is clicked, so Bit runs and lands on 3.
3. Let them try. Students decide if Bit runs before the click (Ex 2), and name the event (Ex 3).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — the flag is clicked, the event happens, and Bit runs: 0, forward 3 → 3.
Exercise 2 — NO, the moves have not run before the event; Bit is still on its home number 0.
Exercise 3 — the event is "when green flag clicked". The hat block itself does not move Bit; it just waits for the event, then the moves under it run.

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: running the moves before the flag is clicked. The event has to happen first.
Make it easier: physically "click" a paper flag, then move the counter.
Make it harder: ask what is on top of every set of moves (an event hat).

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events.
In plain terms: students write and run instructions that are started by an event, like clicking the green flag or getting a message.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read instructions, change what starts them or one move, and explain what the change did.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child knows the moves wait for the green-flag event and names that event.
